title: Chapter 1. Of Sense
paragraphs: When it comes to a man's thoughts, I will look at them first one by one, and afterward in sequence, or as they follow from one another. Taken one by one, each thought is simply a representation or appearance of some quality or other feature of a body outside us — something commonly called an Object. This object acts on the eyes, ears, and other parts of a man's body, and the variety of ways it acts produces a variety of appearances.

All of these thoughts originate in what we call Sense — for there is no idea in a man's mind that was not first produced, wholly or in part, by the organs of Sense. Everything else is derived from that origin.

Knowing the natural cause of Sense is not really necessary for the business at hand, and I have already written about it at length elsewhere. Still, to fill out every part of my present plan, I will briefly set it down here.

The cause of Sense is the external body, or Object, which presses upon the organ proper to each sense — directly, as in taste and touch, or indirectly, as in seeing, hearing, and smelling. This pressure travels inward, by way of the nerves and other cords and membranes of the body, to the brain and the heart, where it causes a resistance, or counter-pressure — an effort of the heart to push itself free of that pressure. Because this effort is directed outward, it seems to be something out there in the world. And this seeming, or Fancy, is what men call sense. For the eye it consists in a light, or a shape marked out in color; for the ear, in a sound; for the nostril, in an odor; for the tongue and palate, in a taste; and for the rest of the body, in heat, cold, hardness, softness, and the other such qualities we make out by feeling. All these qualities, called "sensible," exist in the object that causes them as nothing but a number of different motions of matter. It is by these motions that the object presses on our organs in different ways. And in us, who are pressed, they are likewise nothing but various motions — for motion produces nothing but motion. But their appearance to us is Fancy — the same whether we are awake or dreaming. And just as pressing, rubbing, or striking the eye makes us imagine a light, and pressing the ear produces a ringing, so the bodies we see or hear likewise produce the same in us, through a strong though unnoticed action of their own. For if those colors and sounds actually resided in the bodies or objects that cause them, they could not be separated from those objects. Yet we see that they can be — by glasses, that is, mirrors and lenses, and by reflection in echoes — where we know that the thing we see is in one place and its appearance in another. And although at a certain distance the real object itself can seem to merge with the very image it produces in us, the object is still one thing and the image, or fancy, another. So sense, in every case, is nothing but this original fancy, caused (as I have said) by the pressure — that is, the motion — of external things upon our eyes, ears, and other organs designed for that purpose.

But the schools of philosophy, throughout every university in Christendom, teach a different doctrine, grounded on certain texts of Aristotle. They say that the cause of vision is that the thing seen sends out, on every side, a Visible Species — in English, a Visible Show, Apparition, or Aspect, or a Being Seen — and that seeing consists in the eye's receiving this. And as for the cause of hearing, they say the thing heard sends out an Audible Species, that is, an Audible Aspect, or Audible Being Seen, which enters the ear and produces hearing. Indeed, for the cause of understanding too, they say the thing understood sends out Intelligible Species, that is, an Intelligible Being Seen, which, coming into the understanding, makes us understand. I do not say this to disparage the use of universities; but because I will later have to speak of their function within a commonwealth, I must point out along the way, wherever it comes up, what in them would need correcting — and one of these is how often they produce speech that means nothing.
